title: Domain and range
keyIdea: The domain of a function is the set of inputs it can take; the range is the set of outputs it actually gives. Read the domain from how far a graph spreads along the x-axis and the range from how far it spreads up the y-axis. Square roots of negatives, division by zero and the real situation can all restrict the domain.
familyTip: Ask: what numbers are you allowed to put in, and what numbers can come out? For a phone bill or a taxi fare, ask whether negative minutes or half a passenger make sense. Then ask whether the graph should be a line or separate dots.

visual.caption: For f(x) = √(x − 1), which inputs are in the domain? Drag each card to a box, or tap the card then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: jam a √x machine, squash a graph onto each axis, cut a projectile model at landing, find the hole in 1/(x − 2), keep tickets as dots.

kid: A function takes an input and gives an output. The domain is every input you are allowed to use. The range is every output that can come out.
Some inputs break a function. √x has no real value when x is negative, so its domain is x ≥ 0. In 1/(x − 2), x = 2 would mean dividing by zero, so x = 2 is left out.

On a graph, squash the curve flat onto the x-axis: the shadow is the domain. Squash it onto the y-axis: that shadow is the range. Look for a turning point, because the ends are not always the highest or lowest outputs.
Real situations add limits. A ball thrown up with h = 20t − 5t² lands at t = 4, so 0 ≤ t ≤ 4 makes sense. Tickets come in whole numbers, so that graph is a set of dots, not a line.
adult: Ages 14 to 16. This matches Common Core F-IF.1 (a function gives each input in its domain exactly one output in its range) and F-IF.5 (relate the domain to the context). In England it supports GCSE function work and the A-level idea of domain and range for mappings.

Read the domain from the x-extent of a graph and the range from its y-extent, checking turning points as well as endpoints. For x² − 1 on −2 ≤ x ≤ 3 the endpoints give 3 and 8, but the vertex gives −1, so the range is −1 ≤ y ≤ 8. Square roots need the expression inside to be at least 0. Denominators must not be 0. A model's context can cut the domain further, and counted quantities give a discrete domain.

Common mistakes: taking the range from the endpoints only and missing a turning point; swapping domain and range; leaving x = 2 in the domain of 1/(x − 2); allowing negative time or a part of a ticket because the formula still gives a number; writing x ≥ 0 for √(x − 3) instead of solving x − 3 ≥ 0.

In the lab you feed a square-root machine, squash a parabola onto each axis, trim a projectile path to its landing time, slide towards the gap in 1/(x − 2) and decide whether ticket costs should be joined. The challenge mixes all of these.

practice.prompt: What is the domain of f(x) = √(x − 5)?
practice.hint: The expression under the root must be 0 or more: solve x − 5 ≥ 0.
practice.explain: x − 5 ≥ 0 gives x ≥ 5. x ≥ 0 would allow x = 1, but √(1 − 5) = √(−4) has no real value.

practice.prompt: f(x) = 1/(x − {a}). Which value of x is not in the domain?
practice.hint: Find the x that makes the denominator equal to 0.
practice.explain: x − {a} = 0 when x = {a}, and dividing by 0 has no value, so x = {a} is excluded.

practice.prompt: g(x) = x² on the domain −{a} ≤ x ≤ {b}. What is the smallest value in the range?
practice.hint: The domain includes x = 0. What is g(0)?
practice.explain: The parabola's vertex is at x = 0, which is inside the domain, so the minimum output is g(0) = 0, not an endpoint value.

practice.prompt: A ball's height is h(t) = {k}t − 5t² metres. At what time t (seconds) does it land, ending the sensible domain?
practice.explain: t = 0 or t = {k}/5 = {=k/5}. The ball lands at t = {=k/5}, so the domain is 0 ≤ t ≤ {=k/5}.

practice.prompt: Pens cost £2 each and a shop sells up to 10. Which describes the domain of the cost C(n) = 2n?
practice.hint: Can you buy 3.7 pens? Think about what n counts.
practice.explain: Pens are counted, so n is a whole number from 0 to 10. The graph is 11 separate dots.

pool.prompt: A graph is drawn from (−3, 4) to (2, −1) as a straight line. What is its domain?
pool.hint: The domain is the spread of x-values the graph covers.
pool.explain: x runs from −3 to 2. −1 to 4 are the y-values, which give the range.

pool.prompt: What is the range of f(x) = x² + 3 for all real x?
pool.hint: x² is never negative. What is the smallest it can be?
pool.explain: The smallest x² can be is 0, so the smallest output is 3. Every y ≥ 3 is reached.

pool.prompt: What is the domain of f(x) = 4/(2x − 6)?
pool.hint: Set the denominator 2x − 6 equal to 0 and solve.
pool.explain: 2x − 6 = 0 when x = 3, so x = 3 is excluded and every other real x is allowed.

pool.prompt: Ravi says the range of g(x) = x² − 4x on 0 ≤ x ≤ 5 is 0 ≤ y ≤ 5, using g(0) and g(5). What did he miss?
choices: The turning point at x = 2 gives −4, so the range is −4 ≤ y ≤ 5
The range should use the x-values 0 to 5
pool.hint: Complete the square or find where the graph turns.
pool.explain: g(x) = (x − 2)² − 4 has its minimum −4 at x = 2, inside the domain. So the range is −4 ≤ y ≤ 5.

pool.prompt: f(x) = √(x + {a}). What is the smallest x in the domain?
pool.hint: The inside of the root must be 0 or more: solve x + {a} ≥ 0.
pool.explain: x + {a} ≥ 0 gives x ≥ {=-a}, so the smallest input is {=-a}.

pool.prompt: A candle is 20 cm tall and burns 2 cm per hour: L = 20 − 2t. What is a sensible domain?
pool.hint: When is the candle used up? Time cannot be negative.
pool.explain: L = 0 when t = 10, and t starts at 0. So 0 ≤ t ≤ 10, and the range is 0 ≤ L ≤ 20.

pool.prompt: Which statement about f(x) = 1/x is true?
choices: Its domain and its range both leave out 0
Its domain is all real x
pool.hint: Can x be 0? Can 1/x ever equal 0?
pool.explain: x = 0 is excluded because of division by zero, and 1/x is never 0, so 0 is missing from the range too. Negative x gives negative outputs.

pool.prompt: f(x) = 3x + 1 on the domain 0 ≤ x ≤ {b}. What is the largest value in the range?
pool.hint: The line goes up as x increases, so the largest output is at the right-hand end.
